title: Armorum iudicium. Aiax
titleEn: The Arms Awarded, and the Fall of Ajax — Metamorphoses XIII.268–398
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Ulysses finishes his case for the arms of Achilles. Ajax's exploits, he argues, were shared or borrowed — Patroclus drove the Trojans from the ships in Achilles' armour, and the duel with Hector fell to him by lot and ended in no wound — while his own were solitary and decisive: the Dardanian seer taken, the oracles uncovered, the image of Minerva carried out of the citadel by night. He answers the charges of hanging back from the war, of destroying Palamedes and of leaving Philoctetes on Lemnos, and ends by holding the stolen image up before the assembly: if the arms are not to be his, let them go to her. The lords are moved, and the eloquent man carries off the brave man's arms. Ajax, who had withstood Hector and iron and fire and Jupiter, cannot withstand one fit of anger; he turns his own sword on himself, and from the reddened ground grows a purple flower whose leaves carry a letter that is a name for one and a cry of grief for another.

sentences.t:
Quid tamen hoc refert, si se pro classe Pelasga
arma tulisse refert contra Troasque Iovemque?
sentences.l: Yet what does this matter, if he reports that he bore arms for the Pelasgian fleet against both the Trojans and Jupiter?
sentences.i: And what does that come to, if he tells us he bore arms for the Pelasgian fleet against the Trojans and against Jupiter himself?
sentences.n: ‘refert’ stands twice in two lines in two different senses: in 268 the impersonal ‘refert’, “it is of consequence”, with the neuter ‘hoc’ for the thing that matters; in 269 ‘refert’ from ‘referre’, “he reports”. ‘Pelasga’ is an old poetic word for “Greek”. The line throws Ajax's own claim back at him, as ‘refert’, “he reports it”, shows.

sentences.t:
Confiteorque, tulit (neque enim benefacta maligne
detractare meum est),
sentences.l: And I confess it, he did bear them (for it is not my way to disparage good deeds grudgingly),
sentences.i: And I grant it, he did (grudging belittlement of good deeds is no habit of mine),
sentences.n: ‘meum est’ is literally “it is mine”, that is, “it is my way, my character” — a possessive predicate where English wants a noun. ‘benefacta’, “things well done”, is the plural object of ‘detractare’.

sentences.t:
sed ne communia solus
occupet atque aliquem vobis quoque reddat honorem,
reppulit Actorides sub imagine tutus Achillis
Troas ab arsuris cum defensore carinis.
sentences.l: but so that he may not alone seize what belongs to all, and so that he may yield some honour to you also, the son of Actor, safe under Achilles' likeness, drove the Trojans off from the ships that were going to burn along with their defender.
sentences.i: but — so that he should not engross the common glory by himself, and should leave some honour to you as well — it was the son of Actor, safe in the guise of Achilles, who drove the Trojans back from ships that were about to burn with the man defending them.
sentences.n: The “he” of 272 is Ajax; ‘Actorides’, the son of Actor, is Patroclus, who fought in Achilles' armour, and ‘sub imagine tutus Achillis’ is Ulysses' sneer — the courage was borrowed with the armour. ‘arsuris … carinis’ is a future participle, “ships destined to burn”, and ‘cum defensore’ makes the defender burn with them.

sentences.t:
Ausum etiam Hectoreis solum concurrere telis
se putat, oblitus regisque ducumque meique,
nonus in officio et praelatus munere sortis.
sentences.l: He thinks himself also to have dared alone to close with Hector's weapons, forgetful of the king and of the leaders and of me — ninth in the volunteering, and preferred by the lot's favour.
sentences.i: He thinks, too, that he alone dared meet Hector's weapons — forgetting the king, and the chiefs, and me: he was ninth to offer, and it was the lot's favour that put him forward.
sentences.n: ‘se putat ausum’ is indirect statement with ‘se’ as its subject: “he thinks that he dared”. ‘nonus in officio’ is the detail Ulysses is pressing — Ajax was one volunteer among many for the duel, and got it by the drawing of lots rather than by being chosen.

sentences.t:
Sed tamen eventus vestrae, fortissime, pugnae
quis fuit?
sentences.l: But still, what was the outcome, bravest of men, of your fight?
sentences.i: But even so — what came of that fight of yours, my hero?
sentences.n: ‘fortissime’ is a vocative flung at Ajax: Ulysses turns aside to address him directly, and “bravest” is sarcasm. In 278 the phrase ‘vestrae … pugnae’ is split around it, so the taunt sits inside the question. ‘vestrae’ is plural beside that singular vocative — either the plural standing for the singular, as ‘noster’ does for ‘meus’ later in the speech, or “the fight of you two”, Ajax and Hector.

sentences.t: Hector abit violatus vulnere nullo!
sentences.l: Hector goes off, injured by no wound!
sentences.i: Hector walks away, and not a wound on him!
sentences.n: ‘violatus vulnere nullo’, “injured by no wound”, is the whole point of the taunt: a duel with nothing to show. ‘abit’ is present in form, the vivid present used of a past event.

sentences.t:
Me miserum, quanto cogor meminisse dolore
temporis illius, quo Graium murus, Achilles
procubuit!
sentences.l: Wretched me! with how great grief I am forced to remember that time, in which the wall of the Greeks, Achilles, fell forward!
sentences.i: Wretched that I am — with what pain I am made to remember that hour, when the wall of the Greeks, Achilles, went down!
sentences.n: ‘Me miserum’ is the accusative of exclamation, standing outside the sentence's grammar. ‘Graium’ is the older poetic genitive plural for ‘Graecorum’, “of the Greeks”, and ‘murus’, “wall”, stands in apposition to Achilles — the army's defence described as a fortification.

sentences.t:
Nec me lacrimae luctusque timorque
tardarunt, quin corpus humo sublime referrem.
sentences.l: Nor did tears and grief and fear slow me down, from carrying back the body, lifted high from the ground.
sentences.i: And tears, grief and fear did not hold me back from lifting the body high off the ground and carrying it away.
sentences.n: ‘tardarunt’ is the syncopated perfect for ‘tardaverunt’, a contraction the edition keeps. ‘quin’ with the subjunctive follows a verb of hindering: “from doing it”. ‘humo’ is an ablative of separation, “from the ground”.

sentences.t: His umeris, his, inquam, umeris ego corpus Achillis.
sentences.l: On these shoulders, on these, I say, on these shoulders, I — the body of Achilles.
sentences.i: On these shoulders — on these shoulders, I say — I carried the body of Achilles.
sentences.n: The verb is left out and has to be supplied from what follows: ‘tuli’, “I bore”, arrives in the next line. Repeating ‘his umeris’ with ‘inquam’ dropped in between is the gesture of a speaker striking his own shoulder. Magnus prints a full stop at the end of this line and then a lower-case ‘et’; that is the archived edition's punctuation, kept as it stands.

sentences.t: et simul arma tuli, quae nunc quoque ferre laboro!
sentences.l: and at the same time I bore the arms, which now too I labour to bear!
sentences.i: and I carried the arms along with him — the very arms I am struggling to carry now!
sentences.n: ‘tuli’ and ‘ferre’ are one verb twice over: he bore the arms off the field then, and “labours to bear” them now, meaning to win them by this speech. The one word carries the feat and the plea together.

sentences.t:
Sunt mihi, quae valeant in talia pondera, vires,
est animus certe vestros sensurus honores.
sentences.l: There are to me strengths which are strong enough for such weights; there is, certainly, a spirit that will feel your honours.
sentences.i: I have the strength for such a weight, and a spirit, be sure, that will feel the honours you give.
sentences.n: ‘sunt mihi … vires’ is the dative of possession — “there are strengths to me” means “I have strength”. ‘quae valeant’ is a characterising relative clause, subjunctive: “strength such as would be equal to it”. ‘sensurus’ is a future participle, “about to feel”.

sentences.t:
Scilicet idcirco pro nato caerula mater
ambitiosa suo fuit, ut caelestia dona,
artis opus tantae, rudis et sine pectore miles
indueret?
sentences.l: Doubtless the sea-blue mother was importunate on her son's behalf for this reason — so that a raw soldier, and one without a breast, might put on the heavenly gifts, the work of such great craft?
sentences.i: So that was why the sea-blue mother went begging for her son — so that a raw soldier with no mind in him might put on gifts from heaven, the work of such art?
sentences.n: ‘Scilicet’ opens a sarcastic question: “of course, obviously”, meaning the opposite. ‘caerula mater’ is Thetis, the sea-goddess, named by her element; she asked for the armour on her son's behalf. ‘sine pectore’ is literally “without a breast”, and in Latin the breast is a seat of intelligence as much as of feeling — here it is the mind that is meant, “with no mind in him”.

sentences.t:
neque enim clipei caelamina novit,
Oceanum et terras cumque alto sidera caelo
Pleiadasque hyadasque inmunemque aequoris arcton
diversasque urbes nitidumque Orionis ensem:
sentences.l: For he does not know the shield's chasings — Ocean and the lands, and the stars with the high sky, and the Pleiades and the Hyades, and the Bear that has no share of the sea, and cities set apart, and the bright sword of Orion:
sentences.i: For he knows nothing of the chasing on the shield — Ocean, the lands, the stars with the high heaven, the Pleiades and the Hyades, the Bear that never bathes in the sea, cities far apart, Orion's bright sword:
sentences.n: ‘novit’ is a perfect used as a present: “he has learned” means “he knows”. ‘inmunem aequoris’, with the genitive after ‘inmunis’, is “exempt from the sea” — the constellation that never sets below the horizon; ‘inmunem’ keeps the older unassimilated spelling for ‘immunem’, which is the edition's practice, not damage. Magnus prints ‘diversasque urbes’, “cities set apart”; some editions print ‘diversosque orbes’, “separate circles”.

sentences.t: postulat, ut capiat, quae non intelligit, arma!
sentences.l: he demands that he may take the arms which he does not understand!
sentences.i: and he asks to be given arms he does not understand!
sentences.n: The relative clause ‘quae non intelligit’ is wedged in before its own antecedent, so that ‘arma’ falls last in the line, after the charge of ignorance: the arms arrive only once he has been told he cannot understand them.

sentences.t:
Quid quod me duri fugientem munera belli
arguit incepto serum accessisse labori,
nec se magnanimo maledicere sentit Achilli?
sentences.l: What of the fact that he charges me — as one running from the duties of harsh war — with having come late to the task once begun, and does not perceive that he is speaking ill of great-hearted Achilles?
sentences.i: And what of his charging me with running from the duties of hard war, with coming late to a labour already under way — and never seeing that he slanders great-hearted Achilles in the same breath?
sentences.n: ‘Quid quod…’, “what of the fact that…”, is a standing move in a speech for opening a fresh count. ‘maledicere’ takes the dative, hence ‘Achilli’: the charge falls on Achilles too, and the next lines say why. ‘serum’ is an adjective doing an adverb's work — “late” describing the man, not the arriving.

sentences.t:
Si simulasse vocas crimen, simulavimus ambo;
si mora pro culpa est, ego sum maturior illo.
sentences.l: If you call the having pretended a crime, we both pretended; if delay counts as a fault, I am the earlier of the two.
sentences.i: If pretending is a crime in your eyes, we both pretended; if hanging back is guilt, I was the earlier man.
sentences.n: ‘simulasse’ is a syncopated perfect infinitive for ‘simulavisse’, here used as a noun: “the having pretended”. ‘pro culpa est’ is “counts as a fault”. Both men held back from the war at the start — as the next line says, a wife detained Ulysses and a mother Achilles — and Ulysses' point is that his own delay ended sooner: ‘maturior’, “earlier, riper in time”.

sentences.t:
Me pia detinuit coniunx, pia mater Achillem,
primaque sunt illis data tempora, cetera vobis.
sentences.l: Me a dutiful wife detained, a dutiful mother Achilles; and the first stretches of time were given to them, the rest to you.
sentences.i: A loyal wife kept me back, a loyal mother kept Achilles; the first stretch of time went to them, all the rest to you.
sentences.n: ‘detinuit’ serves both halves: “me a wife detained, [detained] a mother Achilles”, with ‘pia’ repeated so that the excuse is dressed as a virtue — ‘pius’ is the adjective of dutiful family love. ‘tempora’ here is “periods of time”, not “temples of the head”.

sentences.t:
Haud timeo, si iam nequeam defendere, crimen
cum tanto commune viro:
sentences.l: I do not fear a charge held in common with so great a man, even if by now I could not defend it:
sentences.i: A charge I share with so great a man gives me no fear, even supposing I could not answer it:
sentences.n: ‘crimen … commune cum tanto viro’ is one phrase pulled apart across the end of 303, with the conditional ‘si iam nequeam defendere’ dropped in before it. ‘si iam’ is concessive: “even if, granting that”.

sentences.t:
deprensus Ulixis
ingenio tamen ille, at non Aiacis Ulixes!
sentences.l: he, though, was caught out by the cleverness of Ulysses — but Ulysses not by that of Ajax!
sentences.i: He, after all, was found out by Ulysses' wit — but Ulysses was never found out by Ajax's.
sentences.n: ‘ille’ is Achilles, the ‘tanto … viro’ of 304 whose charge Ulysses says he shares: Achilles' pretence was found out by Ulysses' wit, and Ulysses' own never by Ajax's. The second half has no verb: ‘deprensus est’ must be carried over, and with it the whole comparison. ‘Aiacis’ is a genitive depending on the ‘ingenio’ left behind in the first half — “by the wit of Ajax”, with the word for wit not repeated.

sentences.t:
Neve in me stolidae convicia fundere linguae
admiremur eum, vobis quoque digna pudore
obicit.
sentences.l: And let us not be amazed at his pouring the abuse of a stupid tongue upon me: he casts at you too things that deserve shame.
sentences.i: And no one need be surprised that he pours a stupid tongue's abuse over me — he throws charges at you as well, charges you should be ashamed of.
sentences.n: ‘Neve … admiremur’ is a hortatory subjunctive, “and let us not be surprised”, governing the accusative and infinitive ‘eum … fundere’. ‘stolidae … linguae’ is a genitive of the source of the abuse, and ‘stolidus’, “thick, blockish”, is Ulysses' own word for Ajax: it comes back at 327.

sentences.t:
An falso Palameden crimine turpe est
accusasse mihi, vobis damnasse decorum?
sentences.l: Or is it shameful for me to have accused Palamedes on a false charge, and honourable for you to have condemned him?
sentences.i: Or was it disgraceful in me to accuse Palamedes on a false charge, and creditable in you to convict him?
sentences.n: ‘accusasse’ and ‘damnasse’ are syncopated perfect infinitives, for ‘accusavisse’ and ‘damnavisse’, and both stand as the subjects of ‘est’: “to have accused is shameful”. ‘mihi’ and ‘vobis’ are datives of the person concerned, “in my case … in yours”. ‘Palameden’ keeps the Greek accusative ending.

sentences.t:
Sed neque Naupliades facinus defendere tantum
tamque patens valuit, nec vos audistis in illo
crimina: vidistis, pretioque obiecta patebant.
sentences.l: But the son of Nauplius was not able to defend a deed so great and so open, nor did you hear the charges in his case: you saw them, and the accusations lay open in the bribe.
sentences.i: But the son of Nauplius could not defend a crime so great and so plain, and you did not merely hear the charges against him: you saw them — the bribe laid the charge open.
sentences.n: ‘Naupliades’ is Palamedes, named by his father Nauplius rather than by his own name. ‘audistis’, syncopated for ‘audivistis’, is set against ‘vidistis’: not report but sight. ‘pretio’ is the ablative of the bribe put forward as evidence, and ‘obiecta’, “the things thrown at him”, is the accusation itself.

sentences.t:
Nec Poeantiaden quod habet Vulcania Lemnos,
esse reus merui: factum defendite vestrum,
consensistis enim.
sentences.l: Nor have I deserved to be the accused for the fact that Vulcanian Lemnos holds the son of Poeas: defend your own act, for you consented.
sentences.i: Nor do I deserve to stand accused because Vulcan's Lemnos holds the son of Poeas: defend what you yourselves did — you agreed to it.
sentences.n: ‘quod habet’ is “for the fact that it holds”, a causal clause standing as the ground of the charge. ‘Poeantiaden’ is Philoctetes, again named by patronymic and again with a Greek accusative ending; Lemnos is ‘Vulcania’ as the fire-god's island. ‘reus’ is the standing word for a defendant at law, which keeps the whole speech inside a courtroom.

sentences.t:
Nec me suasisse negabo,
ut se subtraheret bellique viaeque labori
temptaretque feros requie finire dolores.
sentences.l: Nor shall I deny that I advised it — that he should withdraw himself from the toil of war and of the journey, and should try to end his savage pains by rest.
sentences.i: Nor will I deny that I urged it: that he take himself out of the labour of war and of the voyage, and try to end his savage pains in rest.
sentences.n: ‘suasisse’ is another syncopated perfect infinitive, in indirect statement after ‘negabo’, with the ‘ut’ clauses giving the content of the advice. ‘belli’ and ‘viaeque’ are both genitives hanging on ‘labori’. Ulysses' word for the marooning is ‘suasisse’, “to have advised”, and the pains he names are the man's own. Magnus prints ‘finire’, “to end”; some editions print ‘lenire’, “to soothe”.

sentences.t:
Paruit et vivit! Non haec sententia tantum
fida, sed et felix, cum sit satis esse fidelem.
sentences.l: He obeyed, and he lives! This counsel not only faithful, but lucky as well — though it is enough to be faithful.
sentences.i: He obeyed — and he is alive! That advice was not only loyal but fortunate, though loyalty alone would have been enough.
sentences.n: The verb is missing from both halves of ‘non … tantum … sed et’: ‘fuit’ or ‘est’ has to be supplied, and the literal above leaves the gap visible. ‘cum sit’ is a concessive subjunctive, “although it is”. ‘fida’ and ‘fidelem’ are the same root twice: the counsel was loyal, and loyalty was all that could be asked of it.

sentences.t:
Quem quoniam vates delenda ad Pergama poscunt,
ne mandate mihi:
sentences.l: And since the seers demand him for Pergama that must be destroyed, do not lay it upon me:
sentences.i: And since the prophets demand him for the razing of Pergamum, do not lay that errand on me:
sentences.n: ‘Quem’ is a connecting relative opening the sentence — “and him”, that is Philoctetes, carried over from 313. ‘delenda ad Pergama’ is a gerundive of purpose, “for Pergama to be destroyed”, meaning “for the destruction of Troy”. ‘ne mandate’ is a negative command made with ‘ne’ and the imperative, an older and more elevated shape than ‘noli mandare’.

sentences.t:
melius Telamonius ibit
eloquioque virum morbis iraque furentem
molliet aut aliqua producet callidus arte.
sentences.l: the son of Telamon will go better, and will soften with eloquence the man raving with disease and with anger, or, being shrewd, will bring him out by some art.
sentences.i: the son of Telamon will make the better envoy: he will soften the man — raving with disease and with rage — by eloquence, or cleverly draw him out by some device.
sentences.n: Sarcasm throughout: eloquence and craft are exactly what Ulysses has been claiming for himself and denying to Ajax, so ‘eloquio’ and ‘callidus’ are handed over as a taunt. ‘Telamonius’, “the son of Telamon”, is Ajax. ‘morbis iraque’ are two ablatives of cause under the one participle ‘furentem’.

sentences.t:
Ante retro Simois fluet et sine frondibus Ide
stabit et auxilium promittet Achaia Troiae,
quam, cessante meo pro vestris pectore rebus,
Aiacis stolidi Danais sollertia prosit!
sentences.l: Sooner shall Simois flow backwards, and Ida stand without leaves, and Achaia promise help to Troy, than — with my mind ceasing to work for your affairs — the shrewdness of blockish Ajax do the Greeks any good!
sentences.i: Sooner will Simois run backwards, and Ida stand bare of leaves, and Achaia offer help to Troy, than the cunning of thick-witted Ajax do the Greeks any good, once my brain has stopped working for your cause.
sentences.n: ‘ante … quam’ is pulled wide apart, “sooner … than”, with three impossibilities laid between them. ‘cessante meo … pectore’ is an ablative absolute, “with my mind at a standstill”, and ‘pectus’ is again the seat of intelligence. ‘stolidi’ is Ulysses' word for Ajax once more, as at 306, and ‘sollertia’ — the very quality he denies him — is the sting.

sentences.t:
Sis licet infestus sociis regique mihique,
dure Philoctete, licet exsecrere meumque
devoveas sine fine caput cupiasque dolenti
me tibi forte dari nostrumque haurire cruorem,
sentences.l: Though you be hostile to the allies and to the king and to me, harsh Philoctetes, though you curse, and devote my head without end, and desire that I be given to you by chance in your pain, and to drain my gore,
sentences.i: Be hostile as you like to your allies, to the king, to me, hard Philoctetes; curse me if you will, call down damnation on my head without end, long for chance to put me in your hands while you suffer, and to drink my blood —
sentences.n: ‘licet’ with the subjunctive is concessive, “granted that you do”, and it governs the whole string of verbs down to ‘haurire’. Ulysses turns aside from the assembly to address the absent Philoctetes directly. ‘devoveas … caput’ is the formal language of a curse, devoting a man's head to the powers below, and ‘haurire cruorem’, “to drain the gore”, is left at its full force — it is the wish Ulysses puts into his enemy's mouth. ‘dolenti’ is a dative of the person, “to you as you suffer”.

sentences.t: utque tui mihi, sic fiat tibi copia nostri:
sentences.l: and that, as the chance at you falls to me, so may the chance at me fall to you:
sentences.i: and that, just as I get my chance at you, so you may get yours at me:
sentences.n: ‘copia’ with a genitive is “access to, a chance at” a person, and ‘tui’ and ‘nostri’ are those genitives, one in each half, with the single verb ‘fiat’ serving both. ‘nostri’ is the plural standing for the singular, “of me”. Magnus prints ‘sic’; some editions print ‘sit’, which would give “so may there be to you”.

sentences.t: te tamen adgrediar mecumque reducere nitar,
sentences.l: yet I shall approach you, and shall strive to bring you back with me,
sentences.i: still I shall come to you, and strive to bring you back with me,
sentences.n: All the concessions of 328–332 lead here, and ‘tamen’ is the hinge. ‘adgrediar’ keeps the older unassimilated spelling for ‘aggrediar’, which is the edition's practice, not damage; both this verb and ‘nitar’ are deponent — passive in form, active in sense, as the literal renders them.

sentences.t:
tamque tuis potiar (faveat Fortuna!) sagittis,
quam sum Dardanio, quem cepi, vate potitus,
quam responsa deum Troianaque fata retexi,
quam rapui Phrygiae signum penetrale Minervae
hostibus e mediis.
sentences.l: and I shall get possession of your arrows — may Fortune favour it! — as surely as I got possession of the Dardanian seer, whom I captured, as surely as I uncovered the answers of the gods and the fates of Troy, as surely as I snatched the inmost image of Phrygian Minerva from the midst of the enemy.
sentences.i: and I shall lay hands on your arrows — Fortune be willing — as surely as I laid hands on the Dardanian seer I took, as surely as I laid bare the gods' answers and Troy's destiny, as surely as I carried off the innermost image of Phrygian Minerva out of the enemy's midst.
sentences.n: ‘tam … quam’ three times over, “as surely … as”, each past success made the guarantee of the future one. ‘potiar’ and ‘potitus sum’ are the same deponent verb twice, and it takes the ablative: ‘sagittis’, ‘vate’. ‘retexi’ is the perfect of ‘retegere’, “to uncover, lay bare”, not of ‘retexere’, “to unweave”. ‘faveat Fortuna’ is a wish in the subjunctive dropped into a parenthesis. The ‘signum penetrale’ is the image kept in the inmost shrine; Ulysses produces it in the end at 381.

sentences.t: Et se mihi comparat Aiax?
sentences.l: And does Ajax compare himself with me?
sentences.i: And Ajax sets himself beside me?
sentences.n: The name is held to the very end of 338, so that the question lands on it. ‘comparat’ takes the dative ‘mihi’. Magnus prints ‘comparat’, an indicative, “does he compare”; some editions print ‘conferat’, a subjunctive, “is he to match himself?”.

sentences.t:
Nempe capi Troiam prohibebant fata sine illo:
fortis ubi est Aiax?
sentences.l: Of course the fates were forbidding Troy to be taken without it: where is brave Ajax?
sentences.i: Naturally the fates would not allow Troy to be taken without it — and where was brave Ajax then?
sentences.n: ‘illo’ is the image of Minerva just named, not a person: the fates forbade the city's capture while it stood there. ‘capi’ is a passive infinitive after ‘prohibebant’, “were preventing Troy from being taken”. ‘Nempe’ is dry — “of course, naturally” — and sets up the question that follows it.

sentences.t:
Ubi sunt ingentia magni
verba viri?
sentences.l: Where are the huge words of the great man?
sentences.i: Where are the vast words of our great man?
sentences.n: ‘ingentia … verba’ and ‘magni … viri’ are interlocked, each adjective parted from its noun and the whole pair straddling the end of 340; the sarcasm sits in putting “huge” next to “words” and “great” next to “man”.

sentences.t:
Cur hic metuis? cur audet Ulixes
ire per excubias et se committere nocti
perque feros enses non tantum moenia Troum,
verum etiam summas arces intrare suaque
eripere aede deam raptamque adferre per hostes?
sentences.l: Why are you afraid here? Why does Ulysses dare to go through the watch-posts, and entrust himself to the night, and through savage swords to enter not only the walls of the Trojans but even the topmost citadels, and to tear the goddess out of her own temple, and to carry her, once snatched, through the enemy?
sentences.i: Why are you afraid when it comes to this? Why is it Ulysses who dares to pass the sentries and trust himself to the night, and through drawn swords to enter not the walls of Troy only but the height of the citadel, and pull the goddess out of her own shrine, and carry her off through the midst of the enemy?
sentences.n: ‘metuis’ is second person: after speaking of Ajax in the third person at 340–341 Ulysses turns and addresses him, and ‘hic’ is the adverb, “here, in this business”, not “this man”. Against that fear he sets ‘Ulixes’, naming himself in the third person as though from outside. The infinitives ‘ire’, ‘committere’, ‘intrare’, ‘eripere’ and ‘adferre’ all depend on ‘audet’. ‘suaque … aede’ is an ablative of separation split across the end of 344, “out of her own temple”, and ‘adferre’ keeps the older unassimilated spelling for ‘afferre’.

sentences.t:
Quae nisi fecissem, frustra Telamone creatus
gestasset laeva taurorum tergora septem.
sentences.l: And if I had not done these things, the man begotten of Telamon would in vain have carried the seven bull-hides on his left arm.
sentences.i: Had I not done all this, Telamon's son would have carried his seven bull-hides on his left arm for nothing.
sentences.n: ‘Quae’ is a connecting relative: “and if I had not done these things”. The condition is contrary to fact in past time, pluperfect subjunctive in both halves — ‘fecissem … gestasset’, the second syncopated for ‘gestavisset’. ‘taurorum tergora septem’ is Ajax's shield, named by what it is made of, and ‘laeva’ is the left hand, the shield hand.

sentences.t:
Illa nocte mihi Troiae victoria parta est,
Pergama tunc vici, cum vinci posse coegi!
sentences.l: On that night the victory over Troy was won by me; then I conquered Pergama, when I forced it to be able to be conquered!
sentences.i: That night the victory over Troy was won, and won by me: I took Pergamum then — at the moment when I made it possible to take.
sentences.n: ‘mihi’ is a dative of the agent with the perfect passive ‘parta est’, the regular idiom, “was won by me”. ‘vici’ and ‘vinci’ set the active against the passive of one verb inside a single line, and ‘posse’ reduces the second to a bare capacity: he conquered Troy by making Troy conquerable.

sentences.t:
Desine Tydiden vultuque et murmure nobis
ostentare meum: pars est sua laudis in illo.
sentences.l: Stop parading my son of Tydeus at us with looks and muttering: his own share of the praise is in him.
sentences.i: Stop flourishing my son of Tydeus at us with looks and mutterings: he has his own share of the credit.
sentences.n: ‘Tydiden … meum’, “my son of Tydeus”, is Diomedes, who went with Ulysses on the night raid; the possessive is the point, and ‘meum’ is held over into 351, arriving only after the infinitive ‘ostentare’, so that it lands last, well behind the noun it agrees with. ‘Desine’ takes the infinitive ‘ostentare’. ‘vultu’ and ‘murmure’ are ablatives of means: Ajax has been pulling faces and grumbling rather than speaking.

sentences.t:
Nec tu, cum socia clipeum pro classe tenebas,
solus eras: tibi turba comes, mihi contigit unus.
sentences.l: Nor were you alone, when you were holding your shield in front of the allied fleet: to you a crowd fell as companion, to me one man.
sentences.i: Nor were you alone when you held your shield before the allied fleet: you had a crowd for company; I had one man.
sentences.n: ‘contigit’, “fell to the lot of”, serves both halves with the datives ‘tibi’ and ‘mihi’, and the second half is stripped to the bone — “to me, one”. ‘comes’ stands in apposition to ‘turba’: “a crowd as companion”. ‘tu’ addresses Ajax directly, as ‘metuis’ already did at 341.

sentences.t:
Qui nisi pugnacem sciret sapiente minorem
esse nec indomitae deberi praemia dextrae,
ipse quoque haec peteret,
sentences.l: And if he did not know that the fighter is less than the wise man, and that prizes are not owed to an unconquered right hand, he too would be seeking these arms,
sentences.i: And if he did not know that the fighter ranks below the wise man, and that prizes are not owed to an unbeaten right hand, he would be after them himself,
sentences.n: ‘Qui’ is a connecting relative — “and he”, Diomedes, carried over from the previous sentence. The condition is contrary to fact in present time, imperfect subjunctive in both halves: ‘sciret … peteret’. ‘sapiente’ is an ablative of comparison after ‘minorem’, and ‘deberi’ a passive infinitive inside the indirect statement.

sentences.t:
peteret moderatior Aiax
Eurypylusque ferox claroque Andraemone natus,
nec minus Idomeneus patriaque creatus eadem
Meriones, peteret maioris frater Atridae:
sentences.l: the more restrained Ajax would be seeking them, and fierce Eurypylus, and the one born of famous Andraemon, and no less Idomeneus and Meriones, begotten of the same fatherland, and the brother of the elder son of Atreus would be seeking them:
sentences.i: so would the other, steadier Ajax, and fierce Eurypylus, and the son of famous Andraemon, and Idomeneus no less, and Meriones his countryman, and the brother of the elder son of Atreus:
sentences.n: ‘moderatior Aiax’ is a second Ajax, marked off from the speaker's opponent by the comparative alone — the steadier of the two. ‘claro … Andraemone natus’ and ‘patria … creatus eadem’ are participles with the ablative of origin, “born from”. ‘maioris frater Atridae’ names a man by his relation to his brother. ‘peteret’ opens the list at 356 and closes it at 359, holding the whole run together.

sentences.t:
quippe manu fortes nec sunt tibi Marte secundi,
consiliis cessere meis.
sentences.l: for, brave in the hand and not second to you in war, they yielded to my counsels.
sentences.i: for, brave as they are in the hand and no second to you in war, they gave way to my counsels.
sentences.n: ‘cessere’ is the poetic third-plural perfect for ‘cesserunt’; ‘valuere’ at 393 is the same form. ‘manu’ and ‘Marte’ are ablatives of respect, “in respect of the hand, in respect of war”, and ‘Marte’ is the god's name standing for the fighting itself. Magnus prints ‘tibi’, “second to you”; some editions print ‘mihi’, “second to me”.

sentences.t:
Tibi dextera bello
utilis: ingenium est, quod eget moderamine nostro;
sentences.l: To you a right hand useful for war; there is a native force, which stands in need of my steering;
sentences.i: You have a right hand that is useful in war — a raw force, and one that needs my guiding.
sentences.n: The first half has no verb: ‘est’ has to be carried over from the second, giving the dative of possession again — “to you [is] a right hand useful for war”. ‘moderamine’ is the word used of a ship's rudder, so the metaphor is steering, and ‘nostro’ is once more the plural standing for the singular.

sentences.t: tu vires sine mente geris, mihi cura futuri;
sentences.l: you carry strength without mind; to me the care of the future;
sentences.i: you bear strength with no mind behind it; the thought for what is coming falls to me;
sentences.n: The second half is verbless too, another dative of possession with ‘est’ understood: “the care of the future is mine”. ‘futuri’ is the future participle used as a noun, “of what is to be”. From 361 to 369 the argument runs on this one shape, point set against point, ‘tu’ against ‘ego’.

sentences.t:
tu pugnare potes, pugnandi tempora mecum
eligit Atrides;
sentences.l: you are able to fight; the times for fighting the son of Atreus chooses along with me;
sentences.i: you can fight; when to fight, the son of Atreus decides with me;
sentences.n: ‘pugnandi’ is a gerund in the genitive depending on ‘tempora’, “the times of fighting”, set straight against the plain infinitive ‘pugnare’ just before it. ‘Atrides’ is Agamemnon, named as the son of Atreus.

sentences.t:
tu tantum corpore prodes,
nos animo;
sentences.l: you are of use only by the body, we by the mind;
sentences.i: you are of use by the body only; we, by the mind;
sentences.n: ‘corpore’ and ‘animo’ are ablatives of means under a single verb ‘prodes’, which has to be supplied in the second half. ‘nos’ is the plural standing for “I” once again, kept up throughout this passage.

sentences.l: and by how much the man who steers the ship goes ahead of the oarsman's duty, by how much a leader is greater than a soldier, by so much do I surpass you;
sentences.i: and by as much as the man at the helm outgoes the rower's work, by as much as a general is greater than a private soldier, by so much do I surpass you;
sentences.n: ‘quanto … quanto’ are ablatives of the measure of difference, twice put; ‘tantum’ answers them, an accusative of extent and not an ablative: “by however much … by so much”. ‘qui temperat’, “the one who steers”, is a relative clause standing as a noun, and ‘milite’ is an ablative of comparison after ‘maior’. Both comparisons are chosen to fit the case being made: command, not strength.

sentences.t:
nec non in corpore nostro
pectora sunt potiora manu: vigor omnis in illis.
sentences.l: and indeed in our own body the breast is more powerful than the hand: all the force is in it.
sentences.i: and indeed within one body the mind counts for more than the hand: all the force is there.
sentences.n: ‘nec non’ is a double negative used as a strong affirmative, “and indeed”. ‘manu’ is an ablative of comparison after ‘potiora’. ‘pectora’ is a poetic plural for the one breast and means the mind again, so the argument closes where it opened at 290, with the man ‘sine pectore’.

sentences.t:
At vos, o proceres, vigili date praemia vestro,
proque tot annorum cura, quibus anxius egi,
hunc titulum meritis pensandum reddite nostris.
sentences.l: But you, O chieftains, give the prizes to your wakeful one, and in return for the care of so many years, through which I have lived anxious, give back this title, to be weighed against my deserts.
sentences.i: But you, my lords, give the prize to your own watchman; and for the care of so many years, which I have passed in anxiety, render me this title as the counterweight to what I have earned.
sentences.n: ‘vigili … vestro’ is an adjective used as a noun, “to your wakeful one”, and points back at the night raid of 342–345. ‘quibus … egi’ is an ablative of time within which — “during which years”. ‘pensandum’ is a gerundive agreeing with ‘titulum’: “this title, to be weighed out against my services”, and the image is a pair of scales.

sentences.t:
Iam labor in fine est: obstantia fata removi
altaque posse capi faciendo Pergama cepi.
sentences.l: Now the labour is at its end: I removed the fates that stood in the way, and by making high Pergama able to be taken, I took it.
sentences.i: The work is at its end now: I removed the fates that stood in the way, and by making high Pergamum takeable, I took it.
sentences.n: ‘faciendo’ is a gerund in the ablative, “by making”, with the infinitive phrase ‘posse capi’ for what it makes true. ‘obstantia fata’ is a participle used as an adjective, “the fates standing in the way”. The paradox of 349 comes back in a second shape: to make a thing capturable is, on this argument, already to have captured it.

sentences.t:
Per spes nunc socias casuraque moenia Troum
perque deos oro, quos hosti nuper ademi,
per siquid superest, quod sit sapienter agendum,
siquid adhuc audax ex praecipitique petendum est,
si Troiae fatis aliquid restare putatis,
sentences.l: By our shared hopes now, and by the walls of the Trojans that are going to fall, and by the gods whom I lately took away from the enemy, I beg — by whatever remains that must be done wisely, if anything bold and out of a sheer drop is still to be sought, if you think anything is left for Troy's destiny,
sentences.i: By our common hopes now, by the Trojan walls that are to fall, by the gods I lately stripped from the enemy, I beg you — by whatever is left to be done wisely, if there is anything daring, anything to be reached for from the edge of a cliff, if you think Troy's fate still holds something in reserve,
sentences.n: A formal oath: three ‘per’ phrases followed by two ‘si’ clauses, with the verb ‘oro’ dropped in among them at 376. ‘casura’ is a future participle, “about to fall”. ‘ex praecipiti’, “from a sheer drop”, is the standing image for a desperate venture, and ‘agendum’ and ‘petendum’ are gerundives of what must be done. ‘siquid’ is ‘si quid’ written as one word, which is the edition's spelling.

sentences.t:
este mei memores! Aut si mihi non datis arma,
huic date!” — et ostendit signum fatale Minervae.
sentences.l: be mindful of me! Or if you do not give the arms to me, give them to her!” — and he displayed the fateful image of Minerva.
sentences.i: remember me! Or if you will not give the arms to me, give them to her!” — and he held up the fateful image of Minerva.
sentences.n: ‘memores’ takes the genitive ‘mei’, “mindful of me”. ‘huic’ is a dative, “to this one”: he is already pointing at the statue, and the gesture finishes the sentence for him. Here is the seam of the whole part: the closing quotation mark and the dash in 381 are where Ulysses stops speaking, and ‘et ostendit’ is the poem's own voice taking the story back. One speech remains inside that narration — Ajax's, at 387–390.

sentences.t:
Mota manus procerum est, et quid facundia posset,
re patuit, fortisque viri tulit arma disertus.
sentences.l: The band of the chieftains was moved, and what eloquence could do was made plain by the event: and the eloquent man carried off the brave man's arms.
sentences.i: The lords were moved, and the outcome showed plainly what eloquence can do: the man of words carried off the brave man's arms.
sentences.n: ‘manus’ here is “a band, a company”, not “hand” — the word that stood for the hand at 360 and at 369 now stands for the assembly that has just voted. ‘quid … posset’ is an indirect question in the subjunctive, and ‘re’ is an ablative, “by the fact, by the event”. The closing clause sets ‘fortis’ against ‘disertus’, each adjective standing as a noun, and delivers the verdict of the whole contest in five words.

sentences.t:
Hectora qui solus, qui ferrum ignesque Iovemque
sustinuit totiens, unam non sustinet iram,
invictumque virum vicit dolor:
sentences.l: He who alone, who so many times withstood Hector, and iron and fires and Jupiter, does not withstand one anger, and grief conquered the unconquered man:
sentences.i: The man who alone, and so many times over, withstood Hector, and sword and fire and Jupiter himself, cannot withstand one fit of anger: grief conquered the unconquered man.
sentences.n: ‘Hectora’ keeps the Greek accusative of the name. The tense shifts inside the sentence: perfect ‘sustinuit’ for the years of standing firm, present ‘sustinet’ for the moment of failure. ‘Iovemque’ is Jupiter as an enemy in the field, as at 269. ‘invictum … vicit’ puts the same verb on both sides of the phrase — the unconquered man is conquered, and by his own grief.

sentences.t:
arripit ensem
et “meus hic certe est! an et hunc sibi poscit Ulixes?
sentences.l: he snatches up the sword, and “this one at least is mine! Or does Ulysses demand this too for himself?
sentences.i: He snatches up his sword: “This at least is mine — or does Ulysses claim this too?
sentences.n: ‘arripit’ is a present used of a past act, following ‘sustinet’ in 385; the narration goes back to the perfect at ‘Dixit’ in 391. ‘sibi’ is a dative of advantage, “for himself”. The whole force of the line is in ‘certe’: one thing, at least, the award cannot take from him.

sentences.t:
Hoc” ait “utendum est in me mihi, quique cruore
saepe Phrygum maduit, domini nunc caede madebit,
ne quisquam Aiacem possit superare nisi Aiax.”
sentences.l: “This”, he says, “must be used by me against me; and the blade which has often been wet with the gore of the Phrygians will now be wet with its master's slaughter, so that no one may be able to overcome Ajax except Ajax.”
sentences.i: “This,” he says, “is what I must use, and use against myself; and the blade that has so often been drenched with Phrygian blood will now be drenched with its own master's — so that no one can defeat Ajax but Ajax.”
sentences.n: ‘utendum est … mihi’ is a gerundive of obligation with the dative of the agent, “it must be used by me”, and ‘hoc’ is the ablative that ‘uti’ requires. ‘qui … maduit … madebit’ is a connecting relative whose antecedent is that same sword: perfect and then future, one verb twice over, with only the source of the wetting changed. ‘caede’ is “slaughter”, not merely “death”, and the literal keeps it at that force — he names what he is about to do.

sentences.t:
Dixit et in pectus tum demum vulnera passum,
qua patuit ferro, letalem condidit ensem.
sentences.l: He spoke, and into his breast — which then at last suffered wounds — where it lay open to the steel, he buried the deadly sword.
sentences.i: He spoke, and into the breast that only then suffered a wound, at the point where it lay open to steel, he buried the deadly sword.
sentences.n: ‘Dixit et’ closes the speech and turns it straight into the act. ‘vulnera passum’ is the perfect participle of the deponent ‘patior’, agreeing with ‘pectus’ — active in sense despite its passive form, “the breast that suffered wounds” — and ‘tum demum’, “then at last”, makes the point that it never had before. In ‘qua patuit ferro’, ‘qua’ is “at the point where” and ‘ferro’ a dative with ‘patuit’, “lay open to the steel”; Magnus prints ‘ferro’, some editions ‘ferrum’.

sentences.t:
Nec valuere manus infixum educere telum:
expulit ipse cruor,
sentences.l: Nor were his hands strong enough to draw out the fixed weapon: the gore itself drove it out,
sentences.i: His hands had not the strength to draw the fixed weapon out: the blood itself forced it out,
sentences.n: ‘valuere’ is the poetic third-plural perfect for ‘valuerunt’, the same form met at 361 in ‘cessere’. ‘ipse’ with ‘cruor’ throws the act onto the blood rather than the man. ‘cruor’ is blood shed from a wound, as against ‘sanguis’, the blood inside the body — and both stand in 394.

sentences.l: and the earth, made red with blood, brought forth from the green turf a purple flower, which earlier had been born from the Oebalian wound;
sentences.i: and the earth, reddened with blood, brought forth from its green turf a purple flower — the same that had been born before from the Oebalian wound.
sentences.n: ‘rubefacta’ is a compound participle, “made red”. ‘Oebalio … de vulnere’ names the earlier wound only by an adjective from the Spartan house of Oebalus: the text gives no name for the one who bled then, and the next lines keep him simply “the boy”. ‘purpureus’ in Latin covers a range from deep red to violet, and what is meant here is the colour of blood.

sentences.t:
littera communis mediis pueroque viroque
incripta est foliis, haec nominis, illa querellae.
sentences.l: A letter shared alike by the boy and by the man has been written on the middle of the leaves — this one belonging to a name, that one to a lament.
sentences.i: One and the same letter, shared by the boy and by the man, is written across the middle of the leaves — in the one case the beginning of a name, in the other a cry of grief.
sentences.n: ‘communis’ takes the dative twice, ‘pueroque viroque’, “shared with the boy and with the man”. ‘haec … illa’ splits the one mark into two readings, ‘haec’ answering the nearer ‘viro’ and ‘illa’ the remoter ‘puero’: for the man the letter begins a name, for the boy it is a cry of grief. Neither of them is named in these two lines — the letter does the naming, and the withholding is what makes the point. The archived text reads ‘incripta’, which is not a Latin word; the second witness reads ‘inscripta’, “inscribed”. It is kept as it stands, unrepaired; these files cannot say whether the fault is the edition's or the archive's.
